existing.description_long: In June 2021, six months after leaving his White House post, Jared Kushner launched private equity firm Affinity Partners in Miami. By October 2021, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund — controlled by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom Kushner had closely cultivated as a White House adviser — committed $2 billion to Affinity Partners despite an internal Saudi advisory panel concluding that the deal was risky: the fund was inexperienced, due diligence was unsatisfactory in all aspects, and Saudi Arabia would bear the bulk of the investment and risk. MBS overruled his own advisers. As of July 2024, Affinity had collected at least $112 million in management fees from Saudi and other foreign investors but had not returned a single dollar of profit to clients. Senate Finance Committee Chairman Ron Wyden opened a formal investigation, and in October 2024 Democratic lawmakers formally requested a special counsel probe into whether Kushner was functioning as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia.

existing.title: FBI Seizes 700 Boxes of 2020 Fulton County Georgia Ballots
existing.description_short: FBI Seizes 700 Boxes of 2020 Fulton County Georgia Ballots
existing.description_long: On January 28, 2026 — one week after Trump publicly predicted prosecutions over the 2020 election — FBI agents executed a search warrant at Fulton County's Elections Hub and Operations Center in Union City, Georgia, loading hundreds of boxes of sealed 2020 election ballots, tabulator tapes, ballot images, and voter rolls into trucks. Democratic state Sen. Josh McLaurin reported the FBI sought approximately 700 boxes. The warrant alleged possible violations of federal record-retention and election-integrity statutes, though election experts noted no new evidence of fraud had emerged. Fulton County Commissioner Marvin Arrington called it an unprecedented breach of chain of custody. A federal court denied the county's motion to return the seized materials. The seizure occurred months after a Georgia prosecutor dropped the 2023 state-level election interference case against Trump and 18 co-defendants. The Congressional Research Service noted the seizure was legally unprecedented, characterizing it as the first known instance of federal agents physically seizing sealed election ballots from a certified election.

original_title: China Stops Buying US Soybeans: Farmers Face Five-Year-Low Prices

existing.title: China Stops Buying US Soybeans: Farmers Face Five-Year-Low Prices
existing.description_short: China Stops Buying US Soybeans: Farmers Face Five-Year-Low Prices
existing.description_long: China — which historically purchased at least a quarter of all US-grown soybeans — effectively stopped buying American soybeans in 2025 as a direct consequence of the trade war. In September 2025, China imported zero soybeans from the US, the first time in seven years that shipments fell to zero; for the first time in over 20 years, China did not buy from the autumn US harvest. Brazil captured an 85.2% share of China's soybean imports, with Chinese crushers booking 8 million metric tons of Brazilian beans for September alone. Chicago soybean futures fell to near five-year lows. In March 2025, China had already suspended soybean import licenses for three major US firms — CHS Inc., Louis Dreyfus Grains, and EGT — and imposed $21 billion in levies on US agricultural products including soybeans, wheat, meat, and cotton. US farmers were storing crops in hopes of a price recovery, delaying cash flow, while tractor makers and agricultural equipment businesses also suffered cascading losses.

existing.title: Trump Signs EO 14248 Requiring Citizenship Proof to Register to Vote
existing.description_short: Trump Signs EO 14248 Requiring Citizenship Proof to Register to Vote
existing.description_long: On March 25, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14248, Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections, requiring documentary proof of U.S. citizenship — such as a passport or REAL ID — to register to vote using the federal voter registration form. The order also directed DHS and DOGE to review state voter rolls against federal immigration databases, threatened to withhold federal election funding from non-compliant states, and ordered the DOJ to enforce Election Day ballot-receipt deadlines against 18 states that allow postmarked-by-Election-Day mail ballots. The Brennan Center estimated 21.3 million eligible citizens lacked ready access to qualifying documents. Federal courts repeatedly blocked the order's major provisions. U.S. District Judge Denise Casper permanently enjoined most of the order in June 2026, finding Trump lacked constitutional authority over election procedures reserved to Congress and the states. Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold called the order unlawful weaponization of federal power designed to make it harder for voters to push back at the ballot box.

original_title: Tom Homan Spreads Misleading 600,000 Criminal Immigrants Statistic

existing.title: Tom Homan Spreads Misleading 600,000 Criminal Immigrants Statistic
existing.description_short: Tom Homan Spreads Misleading 600,000 Criminal Immigrants Statistic
existing.description_long: Beginning July 7, 2025, Trump's border czar Tom Homan repeatedly claimed at public events — including the Turning Point USA Student Action Summit on July 12 and on Fox News — that over 600,000 illegal aliens with criminal records were walking the streets of this nation. FactCheck.org documented extensive flaws: the 647,572 figure from a 2024 ICE letter to Congress included legal immigrants, not just undocumented ones; approximately one-third (222,141) had only been charged, not convicted; roughly 126,000 had only traffic offenses and 92,000 had only immigration offenses; the data spanned 40-plus years of entrants, not recent arrivals; and an undetermined number were already incarcerated by other agencies. Trump himself had separately claimed Biden let in 13,099 convicted murderers, then shifted to 11,888 murderers — numbers drawn from the same dataset but excluding the 40-year timeframe caveat. Reuters data showed ICE detentions of people with no criminal charges jumped 800% under Trump, from approximately 860 in January to 7,800 by June 2025, undercutting the crime-focused messaging.

Critics noted the timing coincided with Trump's ongoing false claims about the 2020 election and came months before the 2026 midterm elections when foreign adversaries could exploit the resulting intelligence gap.

existing.description_long: A federal judge has rejected a preservationist group’s request to block the Trump administration from continuing construction of a $400 million ballroom where it demolished the East Wing of the White House. U.S. District Judge Richard Leon ruled Thursday that the National Trust for Historic Preservation was unlikely to succeed on the merits of its bid to temporarily halt President Donald Trump’s project. The preservationists sought an order pausing the ballroom project until it undergoes multiple independent reviews and wins approval from Congress. existing.title: Laura Loomer Triggers Mass Purge of National Security Council Staff
existing.description_short: Laura Loomer Triggers Mass Purge of National Security Council Staff
existing.description_long: In early April 2025, far-right activist and conspiracy theorist Laura Loomer visited the Oval Office and presented President Trump with a dossier accusing National Security Council staff of disloyalty to MAGA. Trump, furious, directed National Security Adviser Mike Waltz to fire them on the spot. At least 15 NSC officials were dismissed in the first wave—including senior directors overseeing intelligence, technology, and legislative affairs. By April 24, Reuters confirmed at least 20 firings total, leaving sections overseeing Latin America, legislative affairs, and international organizations largely unstaffed. Loomer, who has promoted QAnon-adjacent theories, openly took credit on social media. On May 23, 2025, a second mass termination swept the NSC as Secretary of State Marco Rubio (by then interim National Security Adviser) fired dozens more staff covering nearly every major geopolitical issue, from Ukraine to Kashmir. The administration aimed to shrink the NSC to just a few dozen people. Former national security officials described the gutting as catastrophic for institutional knowledge and America's ability to coordinate complex foreign policy responses.

original_title: Death Penalty for the Innocent: Trump's $85,000 Campaign Against the Central Park Five

existing.title: Death Penalty for the Innocent: Trump's $85,000 Campaign Against the Central Park Five
existing.description_short: Death Penalty for the Innocent: Trump's $85,000 Campaign Against the Central Park Five
existing.description_long: On May 1, 1989, real estate developer Donald Trump spent $85,000 to purchase full-page advertisements in the New York Times, Daily News, New York Post, and Newsday under the headline BRING BACK THE DEATH PENALTY. BRING BACK OUR POLICE! — calling for the execution of five Black and Latino teenagers accused of attacking a jogger in Central Park twelve days earlier. The five boys ranged in age from 14 to 16 and had given confessions they later said were coerced; two juries convicted them in 1990 and they served sentences of six to thirteen years. In 2002, DNA evidence and a confession by serial rapist Matias Reyes definitively exonerated all five men; a New York Supreme Court justice vacated their convictions on December 19, 2002, and the city settled with them for $41 million in 2014. Trump refused to apologize even after the exonerations, telling CNN in October 2016, They admitted they were guilty. The fact that that case was settled with so much evidence against them is outrageous.

original_title: Signal Chat Burns Israeli HUMINT Source in Yemen

existing.title: Signal Chat Burns Israeli HUMINT Source in Yemen
existing.description_short: Signal Chat Burns Israeli HUMINT Source in Yemen
existing.description_long: The March 2025 Signalgate leak did not merely embarrass the Trump administration—it burned a live human intelligence source. According to CBS News reporting on March 28, 2025, Israeli officials were furious that the Signal chat published by The Atlantic contained sensitive intelligence Israel had provided to the United States from a human intelligence source operating in Yemen. Israel had gathered targeting data from this HUMINT asset and passed it to the U.S. for use in the Houthi strike operation. When Hegseth transmitted that targeting information on Signal—on a channel accidentally including a journalist—the source's intelligence was effectively disclosed. A senior American intelligence official confirmed the compromise to CBS News. The Wall Street Journal separately reported Israeli complaints directly to U.S. officials. National Security Adviser Waltz and other officials insisted no sources or methods were compromised, a claim directly contradicted by U.S. and Israeli intelligence personnel. The incident risked permanently damaging intelligence-sharing cooperation with Israel, a cornerstone of U.S. Middle East strategy, and potentially endangered the life of the HUMINT source.

original_title: Trump Broad Assertion of Inherent Presidential Power to Override Federal Law

existing.title: Trump Broad Assertion of Inherent Presidential Power to Override Federal Law
existing.description_short: Trump Broad Assertion of Inherent Presidential Power to Override Federal Law
existing.description_long: Across dozens of executive orders issued in January and February 2025, legal scholars Adam Cox and Trevor Morrison documented that Trump was asserting an unprecedented constitutional theory: that the president holds inherent authority to override, disregard, or suspend Acts of Congress when they conflict with his policy agenda. The orders covered immigration, TikTok, energy, birthright citizenship, and more — each relying on claims of inherent executive power that went beyond existing statutes or directly contradicted them. In the TikTok order, Trump instructed the Attorney General not to enforce an Act of Congress for 75 days because the law interfered with his ability to act. In immigration orders, Trump claimed invasion authority allowed him to suspend the entire immigration statutory code. Stanford Law Review published an analysis in July 2025 finding the administration had advanced practical and statutory arguments inflected with constitutional considerations suggesting Article II gave the president a preclusive presidential impoundment prerogative. Courts repeatedly rejected the theory while acknowledging the Supreme Court had not yet rendered a definitive ruling.

original_title: Third-Country Asylum Deportations: 17,500 Asylum Seekers Sent to Nations They Have Never Visited

existing.title: Third-Country Asylum Deportations: 17,500 Asylum Seekers Sent to Nations They Have Never Visited
existing.description_short: Third-Country Asylum Deportations: 17,500 Asylum Seekers Sent to Nations They Have Never Visited
existing.description_long: By May 2026, approximately 17,500 people had been deported to third countries — nations other than their home country — under Trump's unprecedented asylum cancellation campaign, per Third Country Deportation Watch. ICE attorneys filed over 24,000 motions in immigration court to pretermit active asylum cases by routing claimants to countries they had no connection to — including Ecuador, Honduras, Guatemala, and Uganda. In one documented case, a Russian national and her 4-year-old child were ordered deported to Uganda. An Iranian national detained since December 2024 received a motion to deport him to Uganda four days before his scheduled asylum hearing. In November 2025, the Board of Immigration Appeals ruled immigration judges must decide third-country deportation before reviewing asylum claims, effectively placing the burden on asylum-seekers to prove they fear persecution in countries they've never seen. Roughly 12,300 people withdrew or abandoned asylum claims after receiving a pretermission motion — a 16% abandonment rate. Honduras had only agreed to accept 10 non-Honduran deportees per month, yet over 6,300 non-Hondurans received Honduras deportation orders.

original_title: Trump Repeatedly Floats Unconstitutional Third Presidential Term

existing.title: Trump Repeatedly Floats Unconstitutional Third Presidential Term
existing.description_short: Trump Repeatedly Floats Unconstitutional Third Presidential Term
existing.description_long: Throughout 2025 and into early 2026, Trump repeatedly and publicly entertained the idea of serving a third presidential term, directly contrary to the 22nd Amendment, which explicitly bars election to the presidency more than twice. In February 2026, at a Texas event, Trump told the crowd, Maybe we do one more term. Should we do one more? We're entitled to it because they cheated hell in the second one. The White House sold $50 Trump 2028 hats. Trump aides and allies including Steve Bannon and Stephen Miller openly discussed legal theories for circumventing the amendment — including a scheme whereby Trump would run as vice president, the president would resign, and Trump would assume the presidency by succession. Constitutional law professors across the political spectrum stated there were no credible legal arguments for a third term. On October 28, 2025, Trump said he was not allowed to run but had not definitively closed the door. House Speaker Mike Johnson said there was no path to amend the Constitution for a third Trump term.

original_title: Alien Enemies Act Invoked; 261 Deported to CECOT Defying Court Order

existing.title: Alien Enemies Act Invoked; 261 Deported to CECOT Defying Court Order
existing.description_short: Alien Enemies Act Invoked; 261 Deported to CECOT Defying Court Order
existing.description_long: On March 15, 2025, Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 — last used during World War II — against Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua, declaring it an 'invasion.' The following evening, U.S. District Judge James Boasberg issued a temporary restraining order blocking deportations and verbally ordered planes already in the air to turn back; the administration defied both the verbal and written order, arguing planes had left U.S. airspace before the written ruling at 7:26 PM. A total of 261 people were deported that day — 137 under the Alien Enemies Act and 23 alleged MS-13 members — and transferred to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison at $6 million per year paid to President Bukele. The administration's top lawyers signed a court filing arguing the order 'did not apply' because deportees had already left U.S. territory. Legal experts and three Supreme Court justices warned the government's logic would allow deportation of any person, including U.S. citizens, to foreign prisons without legal consequence as long as it was done before a court could intervene.
